utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Frolich, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Elleby?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Elleby, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President I was going to ask yesterday to tender the diagram which has been assigned number P00283 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say 283, on the basis of the list that was just handed out to me. Yes, the diagram appears there under number 66 -- 65 ter 4942.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, and it just may be something that needs to be put in accurately, I believe Mr. Elleby said during the operative time-frame prior to late August of 1995, he was the deputy chief and not the sector chief. I belive that's what he said, so I think that this reflects a period of time from late August to, I guess, the last day of September of 1995 and not during the time-frame of Operation Storm. I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have it on the screen or perhaps we have it already. Yes, there it is. Yes, that's now on the record, at least also the testimony of the witness is on the record, and the diagram gives no time-period so it is more or less, as you say, please be careful in interpreting it. It might not be valid for all the periods of time of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it is not an objection against admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, just on clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further observations to be made? No. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If I may just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If I may just note that the title say that this is a diagram of CIVPOL structure in Sector South during the tenure of Jan Elleby as UN CIVPOL sector chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it is a time-frame related to a person. I overlooked that and then still, I think the matter raised by Mr. Kehoe stands that when -- when sector chief so not in -- Mr. Kehoe, careful reading now makes clear that there was no reason for correction because it is limited to that period where he was sector chief. Yes. Let's not spend more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Maybe just one additional clarifying question to the when with respect to that structure then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I think that is necessary then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, what -- was the CIVPOL as shown on this diagram the same during the period or different during the period that -- before you became the sector chief?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a little different before I became the sector chief, because we had operational officers, investigation officers and humanitarian officers who were taking care of that item no matter where it happened in the sector. We turned it around so we have the coordinators who took care of all the issues in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being clarified, P283 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, in your 1995 statement which is P214, on page one you mentioned that you noticed -- when you speak about shelling in Knin you noticed a shell that fell 50 metres away from your apartment. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't be sure about the 50 metres exactly, but the first shell I heard woke me up and it went down a bit far away from the house. Nothing happened to the house, but I just -- it made me wake. The next shell and a few seconds after fell that close so all the windows in the house were blown in. But the 50 metres is -- is an estimation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What do you mean by the word "noticed"?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In the same statement, on the same page you also mention the presence of the civilian and military population in Knin in the time-period leading right up to the shelling attack. What was the presence of this population right after this attack ended?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my observations in Knin after the Operation Storm started at the 8th of August when we were allowed to make short patrols in Knin, and I noticed that the Krajinian [sic] military, the Serbian soldiers were gone and there were not many civilians to see anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In your 2008 statement, P217, in paragraph 13, you mentioned that you knew the fires from the Knin town were from arson because of the smoke pattern. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After -- after the shelling stopped, and the Croatian military moved into Knin, it was possible from the barracks to see smoke columns, starting different places in the town. And as the shelling had stopped, I assume that it was houses put on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can we bring up the 65 ter -- I'm sorry, P284, which was 65 ter 4941. Could we turn it around? Thank you. And focus.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is a satellite photo of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And who made the markings that are visible on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you explain what the letters which mark the highlighted areas on the photograph stands for, starting with the letter A?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Letter A and the circle is marking my accommodation during the attack. The letter B is marking the neighbour house who was hit by a shell in the morning of the 4th of August. The letter C is, as I recall, the location of the CIVPOL station in Knin. The letter D is an area of the town which has -- were some damage were caused by the shelling. And the area E is in the main street of Knin where there also were some damages by the shelling. And in one of the early patrols, I also noticed some looting going on here. The letter F is an area who was hit by shelling. The letter G marks some -- some houses who were burned, and this is the smoke columns who were visible from the south barracks. And the letter H is showing my accommodation after we were allowed to move into the private accommodations again approximately two to three weeks after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, sir, just to be clear, areas where you note that there was damage from shelling, how do you know about this damage?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The windows were -- were blown out. There were a lot of glass everywhere. As some of the houses had damages in the roof-top. And somewhere, most visible in the area D, there were some marks on the road who looked like shelling or where the shell had hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did someone tell you about this damage or did you observe this damage yourself or how -- what sort of information did you receive?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I don't have any military education myself, of course the observation were discussed with the military in the barracks, the UN military and they told me this was typical damage from shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did I observe this damage yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we please tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Then P284 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If we could now have P228 on screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's a document written by at that time chief operation officer, Steinar Hagvag, Norwegian police officer. He was later the deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Have you -- have you ever seen this document during your time in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing it when I was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Who was the chief of Sector South at this time, which is the date listed on this document, 18th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't remember the actual date when I actually took over the -- the chief position. I know that Norman Boucher left between this date and the 26th. He were going for some holiday. So I don't remember for sure if I was chief at this day or -- or if it was Norman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you know who, if anyone, ordered this assessment to be made?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that order given.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge about any source material that might have been compiled or prepared in relation to this report?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about any maps that might have been prepared in relation to this report?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you personally ever conduct any sort of detailed survey in Knin concerning damage?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, what sort of training did CIVPOL staff, in general, have?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was various courses in the countries. I think there were about 25 or 30 countries present in Croatia at that moment, and there was a very short briefing when we arrived in Zagreb at the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What was the educational background ever CIVPOL monitors and CIVPOL staff?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: All CIVPOL and staff were police-educated in their home country.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What is your level of military training?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very low. I don't -- I haven't received any military training.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In general, do you agree with the findings in this report?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we have this document tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Let me see, this was number 28 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, P228 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we have P225 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an assessment of the situation in Knin, which I wrote on the 16th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you know under what circumstances what this report produced?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was produced after a patrol in Knin town.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Who made this patrol?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the patrol. I'm pretty sure that the station commander of Knin CIVPOL station joined, Mr. Petrov Romassev, and we had an interpreter with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What purpose did this assessment report serve?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the document was to assess the situation at that time in Knin and to pass the knowledge on to headquarter in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Was there anyone else that you would pass information about this -- from this report to?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would typically discuss this observation with Mr. Romanic at the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you explain what you meant by saying in paragraph 4 of this document that the town of Knin is like Tombstone, Arizona in 1881?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that colorful description. What I meant was that it was quite lawless. I wasn't -- I wasn't convinced that there was law and order in Knin at that time, so everybody had to be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Where did you observe the looting incidents you mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: These looting incidents I observed in the main street, which also was marked on the map we saw before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If this document could be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, P225 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If we could have P281 on screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Where did you see it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this -- this sign on -- on soldiers in Knin, and specific in the situation where my land lady car were stolen, I'm sure the soldiers wore this sign on their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If this image can be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, P281 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In your 1997 statement, on page 3 --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I don't have the 65 ter number with me, sorry. Page 3 in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: -- you mention you had the impression that the looting went on in three stages. How did you know about this? What gave you the impression?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the impression came that when we were allowed to get out barracks on the 8th of August, we visited the CIVPOL monitors' accommodations and there had been looting going on everywhere and it was my opinion that nobody else than the 1st brigades of the Croatian army had access to the town. And as the observations were made later on, and the looting still was going on, it was the impression that other authorities or civilians also did the looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question. You just said that you recognised that image. Now, on the screen you saw a badge with an image and text. Was it that you recognised the image only or the text as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only recognised the image, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you remember whether there was any text, whatever that text would be, above that image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I just wanted to note that the 1997 statement was P215 for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: You mention in the same statement on the same page that -- page 3, that were continuously houses on fire in the area. What do you base this on?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base it on some reports and what the discussion was when there were meetings in the headquarter in CIVPOL Knin, that everybody was mentioning and discussing the fires going on, and I also base it on my own observations when I made the trips out of Knin or in the area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: How often did you leave Knin during your time in the sector?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we first was allowed to move out of Knin in cars, it was approximately once a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And afterwards did that change or was it -- did that pattern remain the same?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that pattern remained more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to the relationship you had with Mr. Romanic and Mr. Cetina that you speak about in your statements as representatives of civilian police. What was the general response that you received from Mr. Romanic on crimes that were reported to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I didn't have that much meetings with Mr. Romanic, but when we were discussing the crimes, he was actually polite enough, but I never got any really answers or documentation of investigation or other policing steps made in -- in the cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you ask for such documents or answers?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I asked for the answers and the documentations, but I don't remember receiving any.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Based on your interactions with Mr. Romanic, how much authority did he have?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my opinion was that it was pretty narrow and that he to ask Mr. Cetina for quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: For what did he have to ask Mr. Cetina, for example?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one example I remember, we would like to take some photographs in Knin to document what was happening and how the town was looking, and he couldn't give that permission himself and had to ask Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Was this permission granted?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was never granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If we could have D179 on screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And what -- what is this document. Oh, I apologise. Before you answer, Mr. Elleby, in B/C/S the correct translation starts on page 8. The translation document contains translations of other documents that are not relevant. Yes. I believe we have the right page on screen now. So, Mr. Elleby, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a forwarded letter to which there was a list attached of the murders reported to me and to headquarter by CIVPOL monitors and humanitarian right action teams, and I request for policing results.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2. That is page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What is this -- what does this page contain?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page contains a compilation of sitrep report, inc-reps reports showing killed people in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Who compiled this list?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I compiled this list from incidents reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If we could go to page 11. That is page 26 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What about this list, Mr. Elleby? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list shows other violations or harassments in the same period and so it's a list of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And who compiled this list?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And could you tell us what do the numbers that stand before every incident signify?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this is the numbers of the incident reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how did Mr. Cetina receive this letter?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed it to him in person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was his response upon receiving this letter?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- it was a very short meeting. I handed over the letter and he read it, and he asked me to leave his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my final set of questions for you are in relation to the military in the sector. From your interaction with Croat authorities in the Sector South, you mentioned that the overall authority in charge in the Sector South was the military. What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mainly base that on that our freedom of movement was regulated by the military, and it was the general impression that the military was in charge of everything that was going on in Knin in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you have any concrete examples, other than this restriction of movement?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's in -- after we -- we moved out, the civilian -- UN civilian police and so the former civilian police station in Knin, some civilian Croats wanted us to move out again. They claimed that they owned the house. And we went to the liaison officer. We had two liaison officers in the military, one in the army and I think the other one was a marine, and we asked for help to -- to stay in the house, but they couldn't help us so we had to move the station out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Why did you go to military liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I remember it now, I don't think it would have meant anything to go to the -- the Knin police.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Romanic could have helped us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, have you ever meant General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, could I ask one question for clarification. When asked about the authority of the military, you said "in those days." Your view or your impression or your experience that the military were in control, did that change at any time or was that on from Operation Storm the situation until you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it can only be an impression, Your Honour, but I think it changed a little. But I left in the end of September, and the changes, I remember, it wasn't very big but there were more civilians in Knin at that time than the first two or three weeks after the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There being more civilians doesn't mean that was then the authority of those civilians. What kind of civilians were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That were Croatian civilians moving back to Knin probably where they have lived before 1991/1992. But my impression was that the thing was getting more normalised so that the military was not that much in control as in the first days after the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I would just like to ask another clarifying question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When -- do you remember when the incident with -- when you had to visit the two military liaison officers took place?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you -- would you be able to remember approximately at which point of your stay in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very difficult. Maybe two, three weeks after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Elleby, have you ever met General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I have met the General.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who he was, because he was spoken of at the staff meeting with the UN military.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What was his position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the talks about him, he was -- he was head of the military in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Frolich. Mr. Kay, you will be the first one who cross-examine Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, by agreement between the parties, I will be going first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Elleby, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay who is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just taking up your last passage of evidence concerning Mr. Cermak whom you described as being in charge of the military in the region, would you say you had a good knowledge of the workings of the Croatian army military system?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever meet General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Gotovina only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at a concert at -- at the castle in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I think -- I assume it was end August, beginning September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how were you introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of invited guests at the concert and I was with them in the front row, and one or two other officers came with the General, and told us who he was and we shook hands and then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were introduced by whom to him? Were they Croatian army officers or were they UN officers of some description?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Croatian army officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So Croatian army officers and what rank were they?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you know them?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did they know you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my CIVPOL uniform next to other guests, ICMM monitors, UNMOs, a lot of different uniforms at the front row.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you introduced as the head of UN CIVPOL if that was your position at the time or deputy chief?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my position at the time. I don't remember the words he said when introduced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. And how was he introduced to you, General Gotovina, as what?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In any other form?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you ever go to the zborna mjesta, headquarters, the garrison command headquarters in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if that place was General Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from spoken of at the meetings in the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. And did you know that that place was previously a JNA Dom? Do you know what I mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. People who visited the region, pick up these expressions and understand what it means. A JNA Dom being what sort of place?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A barrack. And the RSK was there as well before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you go there when the RSK was there?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was a place with a big dining-room and kitchen?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any dining-room or kitchen. I visited the RSK commander a couple of times in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to the RSK headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is not the same place, then I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not the same place and perhaps we'll look at a photograph because that might help you.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 2D02-0067, please. Oh, wrong one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While we're here we'll deal with that. Is that a photograph of the Knin police station; do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. It's a picture of the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could tender that into evidence as an exhibit while it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, I understand no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D225 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The other photograph I wanted to show you is 2D02-0068. Do you recognise those buildings on the main street in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only vaguely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've never been in either?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Do you know what they were called?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Can't take that any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be a piece of evidence I doubt of any controversy. I tender it for -- as evidence if it can be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D226 is admitted into evidence. And I take it that we will learn about it at a later stage, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to policing issues from military issues but we may go into them slightly on the way and I'm going to ask you some questions now about your planning on the 4th of August when Operation Storm started. Would it be right to say that when that event occurred you would have had to consider what your policing role was, because it would have been very different, I would imagine, from that you had been undertaking in the weeks before.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it became very different. In the first hours, and days, actually, after the operation the most important thing was to account for everyone in the UNCIVPOL. We were still after, I think, two days missing an officer but he showed up. So the work there was, so to say, gather the force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You are an experienced policeman, I take it, and I ask that question just for the record because of the questions I'm going to ask afterwards, being chief of the UNCIVPOL at that time. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the liberation of Knin occurred on the 5th of August, I dare say that your plans and strategy had to change again. You had gone from a position where the Republika Srpska Krajina was in control to a conflict and then to a liberation. Three stages within two days. Would that be right that your plans and strategy for CIVPOL would have to change?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you conscious that there was now a new government in power in relation to the region where you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you conscious that the political position had changed in that the sovereign state Croatia was now in control of its own territory?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that it was not an army or a police or a government of occupation, if you understand the distinction, but it was its own territory?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was appreciating that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you start to make plans as to how UN CIVPOL was going to work in this new situation?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't do it alone. It was of course the UN headquarter in Zagreb who was making the strategy and then we would just operational that strategy in the sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were on the ground receiving advice from Zagreb, and in relation to that advice did you receive information as to how the Croatian police force was structured?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having detailed information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From the 5th of August, did the type of mandate that you had to be in the region, did it change?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot insecurity [Realtime transcript read in error "security"] about the mandate. And what we tried to do was to -- to monitor, still monitor the policing and look after minorities. Now the minorities was the Serbian minority, and before the Storm it was a Serbian minority. And as the monitors had moved quite a lot in the sector they knew where to look now for mostly elderly Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, may I take it it was a mistake where you said "and before the Storm it was a Serbian minority." I take it that you wanted to say Croatian minority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And on the transcript before me it says security about the mandate. I believe you said insecurity about the mandate.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were discussing the mandate quite a lot with HQ in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And was your phrase there was an insecurity about the mandate because you didn't know -- you were in new waters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You knew, though, that from the 5th of August with this change of government and a change of control of the area that you would have to be liaising with the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was liaison with the Croatian army military police something that would have come within your scope of reference?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any joint meetings and discussion with the Croatian police as to how you were going to operate and what you were going to do?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a few meeting with Mr. Romanic who was head of the Knin police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when was the first contact that you had with the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the first contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we try and explore it, because it might be important.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're dealing with days of events and it might be important. You referred to the fact that you were able to leave Knin on the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To get out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were only allowed to get out of the compound on the 8th and make short patrols in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you meet with the local Croatian police commander on that date?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it about a week later?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're getting closer there. Must have been a week or maybe maximum two weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you appreciate that the Croatian government had to rapidly establish a police presence in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was very necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your experience as a police officer, after a conflict, the establishment of a competent and efficient police force would be a high property. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we just look at -- a short piece of film that was used in the opening of the Gotovina case, Your Honour, at the start of the trial which hasn't become an exhibit but I will have it played as it will put matters into context. Can we have 2D02-0064.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is there any text involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is text and it has been subtitled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the text also been given to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we play.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Dear Mr. Chief, please allow me to hand over to you the signboard bearing the inscription 'Ministry of Interior ...Republic of Croatia, Ministry of the Interior, Police Administration Knin.' It is provided by the Constitutional Law on Ethnic Minorities of the Republic of Croatia that Knin has a district /Kotar/ and accordingly the police administration should be established in Knin. "Since according to the aforementioned law, an assembly has not been legitimately elected yet, and upon this assembly's proposal the chief is appointed by the government of Republic of Croatia, I hereby appoint you the acting chief until the elections take place here and the assembly is elected, whereupon the assembly will propose to the government of the Republic of Croatia the chief. "Until then I am assigning to you the task to perform any activities provided by the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and the laws of the Republic of Croatia to establish civilian authorities in Knin and in the area of your police administration, in your area of responsibility, you are linked up with the police administration Zadar. "Congratulations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Even though I'm not sure what Mr. Kay is going to ask for, but if we could just have the provenance of this video explained a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is a newsreel taken on the 6th of August of 1995 of the opening of Knin police station. Your Honour will remember it being shown during the opening address of Gotovina team. I do not think that this is a controversial film. It stands as a fact and I'm sure the Prosecution probably have a copy of it, if anyone made any research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, broadcasting company, local, national, Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's HTV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: HTV. That is Croatian TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: National TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Just wanted to place that on the record. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D227 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to deal with a few questions in relation to that picture you probably recognise Mr. Romanic in the film?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking at the faces. Here 13 years after, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. You saw the plaque being presented to a gentleman. Did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. At the end of the statement by the minister of the interior who opened the police station, he referred to the link with Zadar, and that is a link that you would understand. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was the superior police administration to that of Knin and it was the police administration from which Mr. Cetina came. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That film was taken and those events happened on the 6th of August, so that when you arrived in Knin on the 8th of August, and by that, I mean the town of Knin, from the compound, had you appreciated that the police station was opened on that date?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember I did it on that specific date, but of course I noticed that the Croatian police were in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. I'd just like now to look at some organigrams as they're relevant to the text that we saw. And the first is 2D02-0055.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been served on the lead counsel for the Prosecution in advance, and three organigrams I'm going to produce which derive from their evidence sources are not challenged.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can have the first organigram and can it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D228, I take it that since you agree on the sources that there is it no objection against admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D228 is admitted into evidence. As I read on the transcript already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just before we look at that in close detail, you yourself went to a meeting on the 30th of August with the Croatian police, including Mr. Romanic, and Mr. Cetina?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Romanic. And you produced at that time meeting your own organigram as to how you believed their system worked. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you produced that on the 30th of August, there were some corrections that had to be made to that document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Romanic pulled some lines and made some supplementary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why I ask these questions about it is we can't find it within the exhibits. Was it a document that you retained and have disclosed to the Prosecution or anyone or did it just disappear?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid it disappeared. I haven't seen it since I was in the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. The purpose of you devising that document and considering the structure of the Kotar-Knin police under Mr. Romanic was because you didn't fully understand at the beginning how their system worked. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you wanted clarification. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to make an easier cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that in the UN meetings you had of senior people, you've described them already and that is how you learned about General Cermak, that you would be asked questions as to how the local police functioned and worked. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was difficult for you to provide accurate answers?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to you to say that you didn't have access to the laws and decrees of the Croatian government to spend your time making an organigram or learning about the structure of the police force?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is beginning from scratch of course. I would have been happy if Mr. Romanic had handed this paper over to me as he's from the February 1995, so he insisted but he didn't give it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I wasn't interest either so --

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was something that you wanted clarification upon, because you were frustrated in your dealings with the local police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no frustration. This is strictly professional. I just wanted to know the structure so I could structure the CIVPOL to match it. There were no frustrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. You weren't frustrated with Mr. Romanic being unable to make decisions, give you information?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is -- that's how it is when you're in a mission in a war area in a conflict that's -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You accept that the other side may keep their cards close to their chest, do you, that they -- they keep information to themselves rather than to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's quite natural. I think the task is to get confidence and good cooperation so when time moves on you get this information on a friendly matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's have a look at a few matters of detail now. We have the organigram, which is Exhibit D228. The Kotar-Knin police administration. Kotar was because it had a special status, did you know that, Mr. Elleby, in the Croatian constitution?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. The chief of that police administration you've already referred to as being Mr. Romanic. He has a deputy and the police stations down on the left-hand side as you look at the organigram are the local police stations within Kotar-Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise most of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you visit the police stations that were under Kotar-Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only visited Knin station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. And Knin police station had a commander called Mr. Mijic. Did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. It was my coordinators who meetings with Mr. Mijic. I remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know what his responsibilities were at a local police station level?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say I know it. I assume that it was policing matters in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you drawing from your own experience of policing matters in how you approached this particular issue of understanding how the Croatian system worked?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some way you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And doubtless, the people who worked with you were drawing on their experiences.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any experts within your team working with you in -- in Knin on the Croatian police system?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. You'll see under -- on the right-hand side of the organigram that there are four divisions. And as a policeman you will probably notice there that there isn't a criminal investigation department. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I found out during my work with this structure that the investigation was managed from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. When did you discover that, out of interest?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you appreciate what the powers and responsibilities were of those local police stations, what they could do?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what we tried to find out with the meetings with Mr. Romanic and the coordinators meetings with Mr. Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that, let's just take police station Knin because what was good for it was good for the rest, that that had no criminal investigation department?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was a basic police force to do with basic ordinary matters.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And by that, we mean traffic, general order --

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Public order, that's the phrase. And not serious crime?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you tell me that it is so or should I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't know that. I think that because the police, uniformed or plain clothed investigation or not, should go to crime of scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to look at this in very careful detail, by the way. Because it is important in your evidence, isn't it, your statements where you mention the fact that you got no answers from -- from people. And maybe we can look at these details to provide an explanation. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, may I ask one clarifying question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked about there was a -- whether in the Knin police station there was -- whether there was a criminal investigation department and it was put to new a negative and you said yes, which I understood that there was not. In that same question it was included that what was true for Knin or was good for Knin would be good for the rest as well. Do you have any knowledge of that, or do you just not comment on the suggestion implied in that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember how it was in the other stations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether what was good for Knin is good for the rest is not something that you could either confirm or deny?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we look at the concept of that, then, Mr. Elleby. This was a -- what you did discover was a highly structured, organised system, is that right, operating at very distinct levels according to decree and law?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the police stations we have on the left-hand side of our organigram, the names of which were familiar to you, Knin, Gracac, Korenica, Lapac, Lovinac, Benkovac, Obrovac, were you aware that they were the stations for those particular local districts?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Lapac and Lovinac, but the others I do remember and I know that they were stations for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've already looked at an exhibit that was produced in my cross-examination of Mr. Flynn, where these stations were identified, and if you'll forgive me, I will just -- D40, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This again is evidence that comes from the Prosecution, Mr. Elleby, and it refers to opening up of these police stations on various days from the 6th, 5th, to the 9th of August, and can see them named there. And that was information provided to the Defence but used by the Prosecution for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No need to look at that any -- any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it is not clear what this exercise brings us. Although the Chamber sees it, the witness says he is not aware of two police stations. Now what is different after we've looked at it? The Chamber still is aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was hoping to remind Your Honour about that matter and I do so with all due respect. I've asked about these police stations on the left-hand side of the organigram and their status and what powers they have -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not -- of course the Chamber has not expressed any doubt. It's the witness who appears to have no knowledge about two stations, which is fine. There's no -- I don't see what the purpose of this exercise is because the Chamber of course has seen this evidence before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sure. I will carry on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at the next organigram, which is 2D20-0056.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It takes time, Mr. Elleby, which is why we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is another agreed organigram which I tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Frolich. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D229 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is it an organigram of the Zadar-Knin police administration, which is a tier above the Kotar-Knin police administration and two levels above those local police stations. And that description by me of the structure, would you agree that's how it was? Local stations, over which was Mr. Romanic, with the Kotar-Knin police administration and above him the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were dealing with Mr. Romanic and Mr. Cetina who was the chief of Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I think I only met Mr. Cetina two, maximum three times. I only remember clearly the meeting I referred to before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you met him for what reason?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we -- when I or my colleagues met with the officers on the high levels, it was usually to discuss freedom of movement or things we wanted to do, discussions about how who collaborate with the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you wrote a letter in September to him, seeking information about the deaths that had occurred in the region.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you first discuss with him about deaths in the region?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember discussing death in the regions with him before this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Just while we're here now, we'll look at this organigram. And you'll see the various departments that are under the Zadar-Knin police administration, including a criminal police department. And was that your understanding of the structure, that Mr. Cetina had more superior resources at his disposal than Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we'll -- we can see in this organigram that there's even a section against war crime and terrorism. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't seen it before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know they had a war crimes section within the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They've also got a general crime section and an investigation section, which you can see at the bottom of the tree. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know this detailed structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And they had a support department of the crime police section of police station Knin. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that all serious crimes were matters that were to be investigated by the Zadar-Knin police administration whose chief was Mr. Cetina?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that at the Knin level, where Mr. Romanic was at Kotar-Knin police administration, he did not have the same investigation resources as the superior authority at Zadar-Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Are you able to help as to when you realised that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know at all there this was this detailed structure, as you show me today, but of course we became more and more clear of how the Croatian police were structured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's as close as I can get at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, looking at your evidence, reading your statement and what you've said in court, would it be right to say it seemed that you were very frustrated by the lack of information that Mr. Romanic could give you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not frustrated; I was curious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Why he couldn't?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was wondering why he didn't give it to us. But I believe he had his reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever appreciate that he was not in control of investigations?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You appreciated that, that dead bodies that you found and asked to be investigated would have to be investigated not by his Kotar-Knin police administration but by the Zadar-Knin police administration.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, of course. But I still found that he was the key for to us get a move on in the policing of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have no need to deal with any further matters now on the organigram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I must admit that the relation between what we find in D228 and D229 is not perfectly clear to me. Also, because under the heading of criminal police department, we do not only find those sections that you -- a few of which you mentioned, but we also find reference to the crime police apparently in the various police stations, section of police station Gracac, and it strikes me that we've got here six whereas on D228 we had seven. So, therefore, it's still -- I do see that apparently there were specialised units under a heading criminal police department, which apparently was under the Zadar-Knin police administration. At the same time we see that there were local police stations with crime police as well, and it's not -- your suggestion to the witness, which he did not contradict, what kind of a division of task there was between the locals and that the more serious crime was at another place, that at least does not become apparent right away from this organigram. I just wanted to let you know that this was on my mind and leave it to you whether or not to further explore the matter or leave it at a later stage, but usually when I do understand or when matters are clear to me I usually don't say a thing but if it is unclear to me I now and then express my confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, perhaps if we look at a document it might even help see the process in action. Can we have Prosecution 65 ter 4619. I'll deal with this quickly before the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you can do it within the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it will be quicker, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Here we have just as a sample report as I thought the question might be asked, and you can see it actually concerns a deceased Sava Babic, pertinent to this case. You can see that it is from the Knin district police administration, that is Mr. Romanic's police administration, dated the 6th of September to the Zadar-Knin police administration, criminal police department. I don't know whether you know the facts about this pretty horrific murder. It's one that's been mentioned in this court. I can't remember whether it was one that you have referred to in your documents, Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking you detail about the case. It's just what happens to this investigation. There are you, Sava Babic, born, date. And then we see that Mr. Romanic has sent this letter on page 2, with an enclosure from UNCIVPOL, Sector South. To HQ Knin, memo, and it gives the details following the finding of the killed Sava Babic, that there had been a request from the UN of the Knin district police administration. PU means police administration. Information on the circumstances of her death, what measures were taken and in what way the on-site investigation was carried out. So that's this inquiry, as a result of this murder, moving from Kotar-Knin police administration up to Zadar-Knin police administration, to the criminal department, and inquiring of the on-site investigations. And were you aware that the on-site investigations, forensic analysis were done by officers from the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I am aware if it should have been. It should have been the staff from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And putting it in -- in a very simple way, all the forensics, all the technical information, all the investigation tools were to be found in Zadar-Knin, rather than down in Kotar-Knin police administration. Am I right.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I hope that assists Your Honours' question. And may we have this admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D230 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed -- oh, no, we're not going to proceed. We'll have a break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, we'll take a break for 25 minutes. We resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would -- the Chamber would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Kay, could you give us any idea on how much time you had would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a significant moment of documentation that's actually going to be presented in summary form, as it comes from the Prosecution 65 ter list and proposed 65 ter list, and it is a compendium of reports concerning clearing of the terrain in the region. And I hope, with the Court's leave, I can deal with that in a brief form, as the documents speak for themselves, once you've done the first two or three and get to the end of a report and with the Court's leave, that will reduce time considerably and I would say I should be completed within another three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Frolich, of course whether or not the Court will grant leave also sometimes depends on the position taken by the Prosecution. Have you discussed the matter with Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Well, we have not previously discussed this matter now during the break with Mr. Kay, but these documents, we do not object to these documents clearly. They are on our exhibit list. Of course as to what inferences might be made that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I do understand that, but it's just the way in which the evidence will be presented and that of course has its effect on the time used in court. Could I ask from other Defence counsel whether there any indication that could have already been given so that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, an hour or so. I just -- it's a matter of course of going through some of these documents that are here so ... maybe a little bit more. Hopefully, Your Honour, less, but with give that ballpark figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, an hour or less. Probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties are urged to seek to present the evidence as efficiently as possible. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I will bear Your Honour's remarks in mind. Can we look at the third organigram 2D02-0057.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While that is coming up on the screen, there is an organigram of the Split-Dalmatia police administration whose chief was Mr. Sipsi [phoen]? Were you aware of the Split-Dalmatia police administration being superior to that of Zadar-Knin being the third level or fourth level?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this structure you show me now. The only thing besides Zadar I remember is some meetings in Sibenik with Mr. Goran Grguruzin. If he is part of this structure, then I met it, but I didn't know how it was put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you appreciate what the level of control above Mr. Cetina was?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know the level above him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right. Would it be right to say that that is a matter of interest to a police officer because it depends upon the hierarchy or for whom you're working, under whose orders?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the CIVPOL HQ in Zagreb deal with the levels above Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. I'm just looking at it for purposes of information quickly. You can see the various sectors that there are. We've looked at sections, this is sectors, criminal police sector, department against war crime and terrorism and crime investigation department. Just in your experience as a police officer would it be right to say that the more serious crimes are, the further up the levels of command responsibility for the conduct of investigations goes?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we take it from your evidence and the summary of it in court that your view was that the offences happening within Sector South, which you were receiving reports of and your -- your own evidence, was a serious level of crime during the period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were serious crime, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you some questions now about the Knin police station. We remember the photograph that we saw at the start of your evidence. How many times did you go into that building?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have been in that building maybe ten or 12 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to supplement that answer, I was there before the Operation Storm as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. When the Croatian police were in charge of the police station, are you able to give us any information as to your number of visits there during the two months?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the number of visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I see. Right. And there you met Mr. Romanic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that -- not that many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. You say not that many times, and we note your supplemental information before this Court, saying you meant him only two or three times. But your statements that you gave and have been part of your evidence in this court, indicate a greater frequency. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was to meet with Mr. Romanic once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think I only succeeded meeting him that number, two or three times, maybe four, for a little period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to object you have to do it --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and I see you're a bit hesitant, so therefore I waited until you had overcome your hesitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you were going acknowledge me, so there was some confusion. No. I believe this question was asked of the witness during the scope of direct examination a number of times that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That doesn't stop cross-examination, I hope; otherwise, I'll never be able to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: The witness has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and sometimes if you want to challenge such an answer, you put that question to a witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the "question asked, question answered" phrase is used if examining counsel puts again the same question and not other counsel. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
