utterances.text: As a police officer you're used to reading witness statements, I dare say, producing witness statements from witnesses as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you -- do you agree with my suggestion that your statements reveal a greater frequency and contact between you and Mr. Romanic than the two, three, or now four meetings that has been provided to this Court as supplemental information?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is an difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Can you explain why your supplemental information is different from that contained within your statements?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only explanation is that the memory is a bit dim after 13 years, for sometimes I didn't deal with the mission at all, and between the interviews then it comes back to you, and -- so I have been trying to remember the correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sometimes when a witness gives information to a party in a statement or in supplemental information form, as has happened here, it depends upon what questions are asked to make the information or to give sense for the information. Is that right? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, I think in some way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How a question is put, what suggestion there may be behind it, is it -- would it be right to say that now you remember two or three or four meetings, but earlier in time, when your statements were made in 1997, 1995, I've forgotten the rest of the dates, but earlier in time, that you had a memory of more frequent meetings?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say today is I think today that I met with Mr. Romanic between two and four times for the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to go any further into this now. I just want to look at the situation that the Knin Croatian police force were faced. Would you agree that after the events of the 5th of August that the Knin police station needed to be well-equipped with criminal investigators, forensic technical support to deal with the situation that it faced from the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it -- it must have been a part of a bigger plan, how to split the tasks between the civilian police and military police, special police and the army. And I don't know how -- how that structure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. But you would have expected a coordination between those two, the military police and the civil police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you were planning these matters, and you are a police expert, you would have set up a system of cooperation between the civil police and military police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was getting at.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Within that Knin police station that we saw in the photograph, what sort of resources could you see and equipment?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any special equipments. I saw officers and officers and I meant there with Mr. Romanic, and I believe that Mr. Mijic has his office there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The local Knin police station was within the Kotar-Knin police administration building. Do you know how many police cars they had?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or police motor bikes?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know how many policemen were in the -- working for the Kotar-Knin police administration at a practical level because you have administration staff and policemen, at a policemen level?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. What is the normal ratio between support administration staff and active policemen?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should be less than 10 percent I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the position in your country?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the local police -- the Knin police station of Mr. Mijic although in the same building, do you know how many active policemen he had?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Your experience as a policemen outside your own country has been in this area of conflict. Have you been in other areas where there has been conflict?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. I want to look at things such as check-points. To have an effective check-point, to deal with the passage of vehicles and the searching of vehicles and preventing goods being taken on lorries that are stolen, the sort of problem that we're dealing with in this case, do you know how many policemen it would take to mount an effective check-point?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I put a few matters to you, would that -- would you be able to agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sure, I could make a plan for it, but it depends on the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. To have an effective check-point you would need people around perhaps with intelligence to see what is happening and whether people are going around your check-point and taking farm tracks. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Radio communication system?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You would need people on the actual check-point itself, so that any vehicle that was being stopped and the driver or otherwise who didn't want to be stopped could be controlled.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you would need men with guns. And a sufficient number to be able to show the threat of force as well as to deal with a hostile incident. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About eight people, something, ten people?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You would also need someone to be able to deal with communications on your behalf to your HQ, to let them know if anything went wrong. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And these people can't be out there all day. You need a shift system and you as a senior police officer probably have to recognise that shifts of -- three shifts within 24 hours is the generally acceptable level. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you're now doing all the planning for Mr. Elleby, more or less. Could you come no your point. To the point is not clear yet that is that you need a lot of things to have an effective check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've looked at a few things and His Honour rightly wants me to get to the point, and if I said 40 to 50 people to man a single effective check-point against a town in a time of trouble, and I don't mean at one stage but throughout the day as people have to rest, wouldn't seem unreasonable to you as a senior police officer.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again depending on the task, it wouldn't seem unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. The task we've got here, yeah. Which is, as we agreed, a serious task. Yes. Thank you. In establishing a police station in this region at this time would you agree that you would ideally need officers of -- with particular expertise in various branches of policing?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, I don't want to go through all the detail, but handling intelligence, handling weapons, running the show, different -- people with expertise. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you see that kind of expertise being used in this region when you were there as deputy chief and chief of CIVPOL, this ideal system of policing?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Would it be right to say, as you went to these UN meetings, that the feeling of the UN was that the success of the Croatian offensive in Operation Storm had taken everyone by surprise? The speed of it, the speed of their success.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the UN military talking about a very fast and professional military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you consider that the Croatians were unprepared for this victory over their liberated area, that they had not prepared and planned --

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- adequately?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Was that something you considered, though?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. Your statement has within it a criticism of the police officers that the -- they did nothing to investigate the killings. And that was a concern of yours at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, Exhibit P215, page 3, and Exhibit P216, are the relevant statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because you asked Mr. Romanic about what investigative measures were being taken in relation to these killings and why nothing was being done. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because it was a surprise to you. It's not what you thought should happen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if was a surprise, but I could -- I could see or I was not told about any measures taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you appreciate that the clearance of the terrain, the dealing with these dead bodies as a result of the conflict, carried with them different issues of planning. If you're in a war, you plan one way, as there may be several people killed and have you to have a policy for clearing the terrain. And then in the post-conflict situation, you have to have a policy for clearing the terrain. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And that is something that comes within the normal police duties?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time we are in August, in very hot temperatures. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And people killed in conflict and people murdered so that bodies are left, the dead body provides a problem because of the high temperatures and heat and the decomposition of the body. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, this is really obvious. I mean dead bodies in a high temperature. There is really no need to ask those questions. Everyone knows that I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The reason will become clear now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 4950. This comes from a section of documents, Your Honour, that are on the proposed 65 ter lest so haven't entered into the system but arise from this and so what we could do is put it on the ELMO. If the usher -- not those documents, Mr. Monkhouse, but the one I'm holding here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Elleby?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can everyone else see it? I don't have anything else on my screen here but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, if you push the ELMO button because then it does not appear under the e-court button.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's finding it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Document dated 4th August to all police administrations. Activation of civil protection. Did you know that the civil protection unit dealt with the clearance of the terrain in relation to dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met the civil protection in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And this here is a document from the Ministry of Internal Affairs signed by Mr. Zidovac [phoen] about what should take place in the aim of protecting life and property of citizens and legal entities. We see on the first page B, civil protection, and if we go to the second page, paragraph 3, Zadar-Knin is mentioned, and it says: "Immediately activate a detachment for hygiene and sanitation measures." And in paragraph 4, "in the said PUs," which means police administration, "in cooperation with military authorities on their approval, engage in the removal of the bodies of the dead in cooperation with the criminal police. Keep records on the discovery of persons killed. Identify, bury, inform operations staff, burial is to be obligatorily carried out in individual graves at local graveyards." And then at 7, this is an order to the police administrations, that one we mentioned Split-Dalmatia police administration to provide people for the clearing up of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a start of a series of documents of which this is one of the sequence. I ask that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before, however, we do that, was the Split-Dalmatia police administration already tendered the third organigram?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the third organigram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that already tendered, Mr. Registrar, I don't think so, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have been asked to ask for admission of the organigram D20057 which I neglected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was no objection to it, I take it, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Just to mention that on that organigram nowhere does it actually mention the relationship between the Split-Dalmatia police administration and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's similar to an observation I made earlier but I did not raise that as a matter of admissibility but rather as a question that came into my mind and questions come into your mind as well I see. Mr. Registrar, the third organigram is Split-Dalmatia police administration is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D231, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D231 is admitted into evidence. And now we move to the next one, then, I take it that was the document that was on the ELMO, 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is 65 ter 04950.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes Exhibit D232.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections against that, so D232 is admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, there is much evidence further down the road that answers the questions of both you and Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 1642. Is it up on your screen? This is the next day, the 5th of August, from the assistant minister, Mr. Zidovac again, from the Ministry of Interior, 5th of August, to Zadar-Knin police administration. And it gives the order on that day to undertake immediate hygiene and sanitation measures in the liberated areas of your police administration focussing primarily on discovering, identifying and burying human remains, estimated a large number of bodies of people killed in the area. And we've no need to look at page 3, as I will take this quickly. If we go to 65 ter 4551. While I am doing that may I ask for admission of 65 ter 1642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D233 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And 65 ter 4551. And this is a document of the 6th of August, and it's a board meeting of the heads of crime investigation departments, and assistant minister, Mr. Benko, is present as the head of the sector, Mr. Nad, and department chiefs and it explains that what the agenda is, handling of hygiene and sanitation measures on the ground, the functioning of the department for war crimes and terrorism. If we go to page 2 of the document. Page 2 of the document at AD 1 shows the decision made on that agenda matter. Police and forensic services department tasked to work on the identification of dead enemy soldiers, dead bodies of civilians. Identify the body. If identification is impossible, the body should be buried under a number. And there was an instruction for coordination and ways of recording the identity of the body. We've no need to turn to page 3 but this was sent to the Zadar-Knin police administration. We'll turn to the 7th of August --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May have I that admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D234 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D234 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next one is 65 ter 4567. This is a document of the 7th of August from the Ministry of Interior, crime police sector, the minutes of a meeting. People are identified at the meeting. On the agenda was tasks in relation to clearing up the terrain. Agenda decision 1, since in the area of army activity war operations are being conducted it is crucial to carry out clearing up. It is our task to carry out the identification of persons in the prescribed manner and it is not necessary to conduct on-site investigations. And then decision 2 deals with the collection centres under the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the system of investigation under the Croatian police system where on-site investigations would be conducted at the Zadar-Knin police administration level with the forensic experts coming and dealing with the on-site investigation? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know if the 65 ter number was given wrong, but the document that is being shown on the screen, I believe, is not the document that Mr. Kay is talking about. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In the binder that was provided to us just half an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Also on the list that was provided to us that 65 ter is not the document that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's put it on the ELMO. Should we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless I think if you want to tender it into evidence then sooner or later we need the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. What we'll do, Your Honour, we've had to go through a lot of 65 ter numbers that are very difficult. These documents are not together. They are all over the place, as well as proposed documents, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's put this document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sometimes a typing error may occur on an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: E-court image appears on the ELMO rather than what is on the ELMO itself. There we are. We even get your annotations with it, Mr. Kay, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Needs must at times -- And in fact, I have highlighted the necessary part. "It's not necessary to conduct on-site investigations." I'll just give everybody an opportunity to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just to confirm your answer, the on-site investigations were conducted at the Zadar-Knin police administration level. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I have been able to trace -- not me, but someone has been able to trace the right 65 ter number of 4559, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we have try to get it on our screen, verify. Yes, that apparently is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Hopefully that can be seen. If I could have my copy back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One of the issues within your evidence has been your lack of information about investigations, isn't it? Hasn't it been?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this minutes of this meeting, perhaps explain why you weren't getting information. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I wasn't getting that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. Within the Croatian system, as we discuss Zadar-Knin police administration was the body that would do the on-site investigations, because they had the resources. It was not at the Knin police administration level. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. From those orders that we're looking at, the decision was being made that bodies should be located, identified, numbered, and then buried without any investigation into the causes of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Translation catchup.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen these documents before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. But you -- I'll not ask another question on -- on the matter. And then if the investigations were not being conducted at the Zadar-Knin police administration level, do you know where, within the system of the Croatian republic, where the responsibility was thereafter for the investigation of causes of death?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. That's all I need ask you about on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can just look -- Just checking whether we've got an exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that we have it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D235 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the last document I want to look at is 65 ter 1198, the last document on this matter. Dated the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see it's from the Ministry of Interior, the MUP, to the police administrations including Zadar-Knin, Zadar and Knin to the chiefs. It's about terrain clearing up. And it raises the issue that the deputy prime minister had warned that several international organisations, through their representatives, keep warning us almost daily that the burial of persons killed in the course of Operation Oluja has not been carried out fully. And telling the chiefs that they're requested to establish as precisely as possible through police station or members in the field whether bodies of persons killed in the course of the operation can still be found anywhere and to ensure that they are urgently buried in the manner established in the course of the operation and refers to the shorter identification procedure. And the end of the paragraph puts into a separate category those who died of natural causes. In your meetings with Mr. Romanic and Mr. Cetina, was one of your matters of concern the dead bodies that were being discovered in the field?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would you -- were you aware from your position of the pressures from the international community for those matters to be dealt with expeditiously, quickly, by the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I don't remember anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That finishes that topic. Can that be admitted into evidence as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D236, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D236 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statement, P216, at page 2, the statement of October 2005, you record that you were advising Mr. Romanic to set up structures to perform a more recognised policing function. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph do you refer to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a little tricky in my perch here to find that because I'm tied by the ear piece. It is on page 2. But it's for you to set up -- you were telling them to set up structures to perform a more recognised policing function. And it was what you said about that. You told us that that statement was the truth when you --

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- attested by your 92 ter statement? It's what you meant by that, I don't understand it, and maybe you could elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At the time what we knew about the Croatian police work, it needed to be more accurate. We didn't know anything about the investigation measures taken, we didn't get any information, and that was we were aiming at [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you -- we know you sent your letter concerning the bodies that -- that you had discovered through UNCIVPOL or UNCRO records in the letter to Mr. Cetina. I'm going to ask you now about the reporting mechanism that you had to the Croatian police, when you saw crimes, what exactly took place. Doubtless you went into the field with an UNMO, someone from HRAT. Is that right? We've heard earlier evidence.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And records were made by those people and then brought back to the command in Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've seen the situation reports that have been exhibited through you. And those are UN records?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What records of a crime went to the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team leaders or the coordinators in the HQ would contact the Croatian police and discuss the matters reported in the inc-reps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was a document given to them that established the crime, the arson, the fire, the murder, where it was, and what you knew about it, so that it formed a record?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that clearly. Some of the incidents were translated into Croatian language and delivered in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was an established standing procedure devised and put out to the teams in relation to the reports that would be given to the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was not a standard structure for that, only that the -- it was important that the coordinators and the station commanders held up the meetings with their counterpart in the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How often would those meetings be?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember clearly but very often daily meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you say "counterparts in the Croatian police," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example station commanders, CIVPOL station commanders would meet with station commanders in the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So a station commander from UNCIVPOL would meet Mr. Mijic?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how often would he meet Mr. Mijic?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember it, he met him daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what records would be taken by Mr. Mijic?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How would the information be given to Mr. Mijic in his own language, in Croatian, if he didn't speak the language of the officer?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The CIVPOL station commander were always escorted by interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. What was the detail that was given to the station commander? How was it expressed?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The important information was what had happened to who and where and when, if -- if the team or the station commander, CIVPOL commander, knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you take the view, after several weeks, that the system needed improvement and needed to have a -- a paper document provided to the Croatian authority?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been a good system. I didn't get to -- to arrange that in my time in the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you envisage there might be a problem in the Croatian's recording or understanding what crime or series of crimes they were being informed about?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well actually no, as we had good interpreters who spoke the language which were used in the terms in the inc-reps, so even though we didn't deliver written material in Croatian language I think it must have been possible to take the right notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The information that had to be given would be of a location where something had happened, the -- the time, details identifying any person. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree that that requires a degree of accuracy, a good degree of accuracy, to help them understand where the crime was?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to look at Exhibit D57 now with you, which is the Knin daily log police book. This is a document that was entered in evidence Your Honour. Earlier Your Honour mentioned about the size of a document. We've reflected upon that, but this is obviously a material document in the context of this case, and it bears examination in a number of different ways at different times with different witnesses and what I want to do is -- is just look at the reports within this document by UNCRO officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 16. And we go to the item 6495, 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is the first record within the Knin police station book of an UNCRO report of a crime. First of all, did you know anything about this particular report?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's on the 14th of August. Were there any reports by UNCRO before the 14th of August to the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there any way that we could establish whether there was an earlier report from any system within your administration of these matters?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when the reporting actually started. I couldn't get in closer to any date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. This is the first date within this book. We saw the exhibit where the police stations were named in the region. It had Knin, it had Donji Lapac, it had the other stations. Did UNCIVPOL officers report crimes to those police stations?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say for sure, but the structure was made so they should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Next matter, page 26 of the book, Exhibit D57. Number 96 of 95, 16th of August, UNCRO officer reporting two bodies. Was that a report of which you were aware or had any dealings with?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Initially was there just an oral reporting of these matters in a -- in a, no doubt, serious way but more inform way to the local Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think in the beginning because the CIVPOL had a lack of computers and sometimes the power went off and to get to spread the information, it was given verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we turn to page 42, this is the third UNCRO report, number 144, 22nd of August, about an anti-tank mine. The matters about which reports were made to the local Knin police covered what kind of crimes or incidents?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be all crimes or incidents who the station commander found important enough to pass on to the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to page 59, the next one on the 26th of August. Number 193. Your Honours will recollect we looked at this with Mr. Flynn, this particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was from a report not by UNCRO but by the police station commander Mr. Mijic and we know that it refers to the bodies found at Grubori, which was a matter of which you were aware of the crime that happened there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in details. I do remember the name of the place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Not the details. But we know from the evidence in this case, actually, that reports were made and somehow information must have come to the local police, because Mr. Mijic is recorded here rather than any UN person in relation to this matter. Are you able to help us further in relation to the reporting of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I am. I don't remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Fair enough. It was a matter that arose through another witness and I was seeing if you could help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to page 70, number 219, 29th of August, Ljiljana Buvac, UNCRO translator, reported a particular body that was found. This incident that is recorded here, was that something that you were aware of or knew about?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the first name of the interpreter, but I don't remember this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. There are in this book another one, two, three, four, five such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to delay -- go through too long on the same theme of a matter unless the Court would like to see those particular matters that were recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I was just thinking about the last entry you paid attention to, the report by an UNCRO translator, where earlier it seemed that your questioning was very much focussing on not being able to do any on-site investigation to establish the cause of death. Here I see that a natural cause of death was established as a result of the action taken. So I'm -- again I'm just drawing your attention to -- that is what I read at this moment which of course I have to try to fit into the entirety of the evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And to assist the Court, because we're going at a pace with a lot of information, the distinction between natural causes of death and death during the conflict was the manner of burial, dealing with the body, one through a system, if you like, and another means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that earlier that if people died as a natural cause of death that was part of one of the documents that you have shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter which comes to my mind here is not whether it's important to know whether someone died of a natural cause or in any other way, but at least there was a physician here who established what the cause of death was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Page 35 in the second part of this book. We're not going backwards. The Court may remember that it was only half uploaded the first time when that issue was raised. The whole document has now been uploaded into the e-court. It's part two of the continuing log. Incident 313, an UNCIVPOL officer reporting finding a particular body on the 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that a matter that you knew about or had any dealings with?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the number of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 35.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. And there are only three more reports in this book in the currency of its life. And the question I want to ask you is: Why aren't there more UNCRO/UNCIVPOL reports within it? Are you able to help?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I haven't seen this -- this book before now. I didn't know of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't know what -- what the idea with the book was from the Croatian police side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a daily log of incidents reported --

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to them and as we've seen it has got some UNCRO/UNCIVPOL reports.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But not really that many.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the question I ask is if you know of any reason why.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That deals with this bit of evidence, Your Honour, and I won't go any further into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to change subjects. Was there a question that Court wanted to ask about this document while it is on the monitor and uploaded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have at least one question. Mr. Kay has drawn your attention to the fact that there is a very limited number of UNCIVPOL or even UNCRO reports of dead people. Mr. Kay, could you please assist me? It was seven or eight in total of all the UN --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 16 all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the time-frame for this log.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From the -- the log itself is from the opening of the police station on the 6th of August until the second part of the book terminated in the 7th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, from what you know about reporting, is it a possibility that in the totality that is UNCRO, UNCIVPOL but also including interpreters that came and reported matters, that only 16 such incidents were reported to the police station in a period of approximately two months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there must have been reported a lot more than that. And I think I can elaborate a little bit about that interpreter. She wouldn't have been there alone. She is the name which got into the book. She must have been there with either an UNMO or a CIVPOL officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now to the joint UNCIVPOL and Croatian police agreements to work together, and a document has been exhibited through you with 11 points of -- of agreement between the two forces. We've heard that on one such joint patrol that the Croatian police car was said to have run out of petrol and couldn't continue. Was that something that you were aware of, that -- was that something that came under your scrutiny, if you like?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. There weren't many, if any, joint patrols, and the reason given for that that could not be possible were many, and this could be one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they that badly resourced, from what you could see, in relation to their vehicles, fuel, the facilities at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Were you aware of the fact that the Zadar-Knin police administration actually kept a full and detailed record of the number of bodies, corpses found, whilst clearing the terrain?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You sent your letter on the 7th of September asking for information and disclosing those bodies and corpses that your officers had seen in their duty. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know that there was a system whereby Mr. Cetina, at the Zadar-Knin police administration, regularly reported to the Ministry of Interior, civilian defence department, with the details of the bodies found on the terrain?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those orders that we looked at and those minutes of the meeting that established that bodies had to be found, identified, and then buried, you were not aware of a log that was kept on a regular basis of that information by the Zadar-Knin police station -- police administration?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, these documents are in that find that that's been put into everyone's hands today. The Bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In our hands, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is in your agent's hand, Mr. Monkhouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it is the hands of the Prosecutor and my learned friends I want to save court time and not labour a point, because I know that the witness won't be able to give us any evidence about the matter, but it's relevant to his testimony in relation to him being not given information by the officers that he was dealing with. And, Your Honour, this file that has been prepared comes from the various 65 ter lists that there have been, including the proposed list and I have included what we have found within that into this, because this evidence is in -- out there in the trial and available but needs to be put into a single place, otherwise it is difficult to follow. And Your Honours will see, flicking through it, the tables and the records concerning the deceased people in line with those orders from the Ministry of Interior about the recording of deceased people found. The period this file covers is from the 7th of August until the end of the year. Your Honour will see that there is a number in these charts on the left-hand side. In the middle, next to that, in the second column, is a second number which is a body tag number, and if I may be permitted this, I don't think anyone will object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that whenever Mr. Kay is saying something that upsets you that you will jump up immediately, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I deliberately try not to upset anybody in this courtroom, my lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in England judges are lords, not in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have I slipped into -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And also the status of soldier or civilian, as well as where appropriate, name, the sex, the place, and then the place of burial, all in line with those documents that I took the Court through this afternoon concerning the orders from the Ministry of Defence how to deal with bodies found during the conflict and afterwards. At the end of this file is a report dated the 9th of January, 1996, which is a summary of what goes before. May I say I haven't been able to check every document and know that we've got every document, as they have come in a piecemeal form. One stage of disclosures has produced some on the 65 ter and then later ones have fed in doubtless whilst the investigations that have been ongoing have produced further documents, and we have done our best in the system that there is to put together what there is. And what it shows, Your Honour, is the system working in a way as prescribed by the Ministry of Interior as by the Zadar-Knin police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is argument, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The reason why I'm trying to save court time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. I am not blaming you for that. We see at least that we find here records, which at first sight, seem to correspond with -- for example, one of the instructions that everybody should be registered. I can't see -- I see 469. Whether there were 469 or some were invented or 1500, I don't know, so therefore whether it is a nine or not, but at least it looks at first sight as if this is the type of reporting as ordered in some of the documents we saw before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I am trying to save one hour of cross-examination, which I hope finds favour and is a more positive exercise in the interest of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask, is there any -- Ms. Frolich, this seems to be a -- a set of a lot of documents which all deal with clearing the terrain, how the authorities both in the administration and in practice, may have dealt with dead bodies found on the terrain. Is there any objection against admission of this material?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, again, Your Honour, there is no objection against the admission of documents. Again any argument be made about the documents, I would of course not make any remarks at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I take it that it needs further analysis. And finally, even if you would have analysed it, I do not think that this witness could help us a great deal in resolving any dispute about what we find in this -- in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you. I just have an additional point to make. These documents were provided to us during the last break, and I'm not at this point quite certain if we have had time to check if all of these documents were indeed on the Prosecution additional exhibit list but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You reserve your position in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you still have to do a lot of verification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it seems that as a matter of principle the Prosecution does not oppose the procedure proposed by you but at the same time they are claiming that they need a bit more time to verify whether they would not object not against the system but against certain documents. So, therefore on the basis of that, I suggest that we not proceed at this moment but take a break, but at least after the break then proceed as suggested by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It may well be that my cross-examination will come to a very early conclusion now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you say, well, within the next seven minutes, then I would like you to finish now. But if you say it will certainly take us ten minutes or more, then I would like to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would just like to see where I am, thank you very much, Your Honour, in terms of what else I need to deal with or challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you would rather do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very well. Then we have a break now and resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before we proceed, I'd just like to clarify the status at this moment of the Prosecution exhibit list for this witness. We have dealt and we have decided on P225, on P228, P281, P283, and I think also P284, if I remember well. Now, Ms. Frolich, I take it that all the rest where you have not specifically dealt with that on the basis of the questions you've put to the witness, when we still had to decide by the objections raised by Mr. Kehoe about the two series of documents, that on that basis you want to tender the remainder of this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not explicitly said yet. That also, means Mr. Kehoe, that that might be relevant for cross-examination. We have denied your objections as -- of a rather general nature. If there is anything very specific for one document or another so that you say this document, we object because the signature we find is quite different from all the other signatures of apparently the same person, then of course, we would like to hear. Otherwise, the Chamber is inclined admit theses in evidence and it is of course with the cross-examination important to know what is in evidence and what is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I understood that basically that -- those are the parameters. Just to meet some of these documents we will present them across the bar table after consultation with the Office of the Prosecutor some reports concerning these investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If during your cross-examination if there's any challenge to any specific documents, we'll find out, but counsel should, unless they specifically address a specific matter on one of these documents, should work at this moment on the basis that these documents will be admitted into evidence, the remainder on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for the break as it gave time to review. I have dealt with all the issues that I could have dealt with, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just remains about the admission of the bundle 65 ters which are printed out and Mr. Monkhouse has. They're all Prosecution documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, which of course is as such not a reason. If that would be the criteria, Mr. Kay, then I would never ask you again whether there would any objections against -- So I take it that I think earlier you want -- as a matter of fact you want to tender them from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And some time will be given to Ms. Frolich to -- I don't know whether you have made up your mind already on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we just wanted time to check the ERN numbers. In fact these were documents -- we have no objection to these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time of course the parties should be aware that if these bundles of documents are admitted in evidence without any questions, not introduced through a witness or -- the Chamber will analyse them and will analyse them with our own critical mind even if that would be on matters which are you not seeking to have this material admitted for. That's, I would say, documents are there, no challenge of their authenticity. That means that the Chamber will consider these documents as contemporaneous documents and that we'll read them, interpret them of course after having heard all the arguments in your later submissions on the matters, but that is the system so to that extent it more or less has become a file --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on which the Chamber can rely in whatever the determinations the Chamber will have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was the purpose of doing it this way. Your Honour, may I also say that because some of these are proposed 65 ters, translations still have to be linked through them and obviously the Prosecution will be doing that, as they're their documents. I wouldn't be translating those documents. It would be obviously be proper for them to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, may we take it that you take care of --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are taking care of the translations. I believe that the process is well under way if not -- I couldn't say if it is completed by now but it's certainly being taken care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course before a final decision will be taken on it, then of course we'll have to check at that moment also whether there are translations. Then, this therefore concludes your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That concludes matters and we can return to this at an appropriate juncture. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is next? Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Elleby, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just need a lectern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Kay for the use of his lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess it is now good evening, Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, I'd like to go over some things that were identified as being in the compilation of documents that were submitted through you by the Prosecution, and the first document I'd like Mr. Registrar to pull up is 65 ter number 2800 which I believe has been marked as P248 in the dossier. Just for reference if we could go to the next page of that document, just to make sure I have the same ... Yes, that's it. This is an UNCIVPOL weekly report and the date of the report is -- it appears to be September 4th through September 9th of 1995, roughly a month after Operation Storm began. Is that correct Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And would this -- would these documents routinely be done by UNCIVPOL on a weekly basis, summaries, at this time?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say for sure. I remember they came regularly, these situation reports from the HQ in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to please focus on the last third of the document where it begins co-location. If we could zoom on that, please, a little bit more. Thank you. Mr. Kay was discussing the issue relating to the cooperation and work between the Croatian police and the UNCIVPOL and at least as far as this document is concerned about a month after Operation Storm the documents states: "Co-location with the Croatian police, policija cannot be implemented at present because the policija itself has not assumed a well-defined structure in the newly recovered jurisdictions." I'm pausing for the interpreters, Mr. Elleby. "UNCIVPOL is business figuring out the policija organisation being set up, in terms of its various branches and their chain of command. Cooperation with the policija to a satisfactory degree also has to be worked out. The understanding of cooperation reached with UNCIVPOL at the Croatian Ministry of Interior level significantly differs from that at the regional levels and even more from what is actually practiced. Cooperation from Croatian officials as envisioned by the Akashi-Sarinic agreement of 6th August is not forthcoming. Nevertheless, a positive development has been the start of joint UNCIVPOL policija patrolling in the region on a regular basis." Now, Mr. Elleby, that summary, can that essentially define what the situation was at least for you on the ground when you were in Knin at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it gives a good picture of how it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So there was some functioning but there was a lack of coordination and basically because UNCIVPOL really didn't understand how the police organisation was set up. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender P248 unless the Court has any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is P248. We received a note, Your Honour -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess before you answer, we received a note that these documents had been marked. I'm not sure if they were marked as MFIs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that I said approximately ten minutes ago that counsel should work on the basis of the remainder of the documents. I had not mentioned yet that they would be admitted into evidence, but they are formally not admitted into evidence. I could see where we would change that right away, but just as you do some verification, the Chamber might want to do some verification as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before finally deciding, but we are not far away from admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I guess for all purposes it has been identified in the list provided to us as P248 so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P248 will then be part of the totality of these documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Elleby --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If the usher could pull up, please, it is P230 which is 65, 22130. The usher. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar. And if we could go to page 2, please. I'd like to zoom -- before we zoom in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby this is document, another UNCIVPOL headquarters weekly report dated August 21st through the 26th of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please zoom toward in the bottom quarter. There's a sentence that begins "almost."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, SN and SS mean Sectors North and South, correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm reading here: "Almost total freedom of movement in sharp contrast to the conditions that existed during RSK control," and you know RSK means Republika Srpska Krajina, correct, Mr. Elleby?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. "Of the same area has enabled UNCIVPOL supplemented by human rights action teams to perform extensive human rights monitoring." Now at least as of August 21st through 26th, the week of this report, as far as you know in Sector South as far as you were aware personally UNCIVPOL had almost total freedom of movement. Is that an accurate assessment?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then on the second page of that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Under section B --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on section B, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's a discussion of restrictions on freedom of movement. And just for the Court's reference, SE is Sector East, SW is Sector West, but for our purposes SN, Sector North, and SS Sector, South, are what's relevant. Sector North describes almost total freedom of movement, and I won't get into the specifics but in Sector South the same general condition as in Sector North, so if there was restrictions of freedom of movement they would have been noted in this part of the report. Correct, Mr. Elleby?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to P230 I guess the same. Moving it into evidence subject to what the ultimate decision will be after agreement on the documents, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties with the last answer. The freedom of movement in Sector South apparently was the same general condition as in Sector North. So freedoms of movement are described for Sector North in a rather general way and also referring to certain roads, so it doesn't give that much information on what happened in Sector South because it says exceptional, certain areas, frequent check-points. So it doesn't give --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will follow up, Your Honour, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, had there been specific restrictions on freedom of movement as far as you're aware, would they have been noted under the report for Sector South under b, restrictions and freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they would have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on, please, to P241. Actually, before we go out of there, I'm sorry, we'll stick with P230, if we could go to page 8. On page 8. And at the top of page eight, there's a paragraph that begins while: "While being critical of the Croatian government, inter alia, the policija's lack of effectiveness in curbing human rights violations, it is at the same time important to appreciate that freedom of movement and field of observation have at least been provided so that UNCIVPOL and other related international agencies can considerably perform human rights monitoring. This capability had been largely denied in the last period of the RSK control of Sector South and Sector North and still is in Sector East." Mr. Elleby, comparing the situation as it was before Operation Storm and after Operation Storm, you would agree with me that as far as your abilities as UNCIVPOL to move around and to monitor and to report, it was a night-and-day situation, correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you compare to the last two weeks before Operation Storm and after, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Meaning that I guess just to be clear, when the territory was under the control of the RSK, you had limited or no freedom of movement compared to what you had after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The movement was randomly restricted under the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could move to P241, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just trying to understand that whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the latter part of the paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can explain that if the Court would like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, seek explanation seems to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, the latter part of page eight of that document discusses refugees coming from Bosnia and Vojvodina into Croatia, those were areas under Serb control, were they not? Vojvodina was part of what was then called still Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vojvodina is now a part of Serbia neighboring Sector East, so to say, on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So in essence if you can tell me if you can agree with my conclusion that the contrast this particular report is making between the areas in which presumably these are Serbian controlled areas where human rights monitoring has been completely blocked compared to the situation in Croatia at the time is again a night-and-day situation?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But on this matter it would be speculation from my side, so I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P241.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just ask for -- the last sentence of this report is -- no, the semi-last sentence is not specific as far as areas are concerned, which is confusing in view of the preceding sentences. It reads: "The uneasy conclusion is that human rights situations in the theatre kept out of our view may be equally, if not more, disturbing that what we are being permitted to observe." And then it adds: "The attached crime statistics should therefore always be read keeping in mind that our monitoring is not uniformly applied throughout the theatre." If I read the previous sentences, that seems to clearly indicate that Sector South is among the better areas. Nevertheless the conclusion which we find under the heading, and that's what we find on page 7, overall assessment and conclusions, the conclusion is not specific for certain areas. I don't know whether you could comment on this reporting and could assist me in now understanding whether that last sentence which does not specify any regions, whether that would be a general conclusion despite what is said before still covering the whole of the theatre or whether I should read that to refer to only those portions of the theatre that are earlier specifically mentioned as being the areas which are bad. If you know, please tell me; if you don't know, please tell me as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I don't think I can put any more details into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me try a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you presume to know, Mr. Elleby, what theatre refers to? Would it the whole country, would it be the whole region?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I far I interpret it, it means the whole area of responsibility for the UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It means all the sectors as defined and that is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time the three sectors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to P241. Actually, I won't move on to P241, Your Honours, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, while you were in Knin how often did you have an opportunity to get outside of basically the city limits or the general area of Knin in your work?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we got the freedom of movement, I could actually go when I wanted, so to say. But usually I went out once, maybe twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And where would you go when you would leave?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go to Zagreb, to Sibenik, or to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were you ever out in the field doing any investigating or any observing?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's fair to state that as far as you know, you never have witnessed any kind of either mop-up operations or -- either HV or special police operations in the field?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to state that your statement, P215 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go to that, please. Page 4. It's the statement dated 10 October 2005. I'm sorry. Which is P216, I'm sorry, 2-1-6. If we could focus in on the last two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mention and let me know if you're there, Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence of that paragraph that begins: "I saw the special police in Knin and there were occasions when our teams were restricted by the special police," before we get into the second part of that sentence, when did you see the special police in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a date or time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it in August or September?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- how did you know that it was the special police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had different uniforms than the normal Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what uniforms were those?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember it a little more military, like what you call it suits or ... dark green, black, instead of the blue that the police were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you remember their uniforms as being dark green and black?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, they were different to look at than normal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any specific coloured beret or headgear?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they wore a cap, a soft cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: A soft cap?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you recall the colour?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think it was green or dark, dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what part of their uniform was black?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this. I think the whole uniform was -- was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that looked to you like it might have black?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it could have been, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
